sources.entry: Open Guide to Amazon Web Services *(GitHub)*
open-guides/og-aws: a practical guide to AWS

summary.one_liner: A community-written, in-progress guide to Amazon Web Services that collects practical tips, gotchas, service comparisons, and links for engineers who use AWS.
summary.what_it_does: The guide is organized as a set of Markdown sections covering general AWS concepts, when to use AWS versus alternatives, and a table of specific services (EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, and about 50 more) with Basics, Tips, and Gotchas columns. A color-coded legend marks official docs, important tips, serious and regular gotchas, undocumented features, lock-in risks, non-AWS alternatives, and cost issues. It includes a service-by-service comparison matrix against Google Cloud, Azure, open source, and OpenStack, plus a product maturity table listing first release dates and compliance (HIPAA, PCI-DSS) and CLI support. Other sections cover regions and availability zones, support tiers, service limits, and AWS certifications. The README says the guide is an early draft, with many entries still incomplete and marked for improvement.
use_cases: deciding whether AWS fits a company's needs
comparing AWS services with Google Cloud or Azure equivalents
checking service maturity and release dates
spotting lock-in and cost pitfalls before adopting an AWS service
looking up quick gotchas for EC2, S3, RDS, or Lambda
notable: Color-coded legend flagging serious versus regular gotchas, lock-in risk, cost issues, and folklore features
Service matrix mapping AWS services to Google Cloud, Azure, open source, and OpenStack equivalents
Product maturity table with first release dates, CLI support, and HIPAA/PCI-DSS compliance flags
Explicit discussion of when AWS is and is not the right choice, with alternatives like Heroku and Digital Ocean
caveats: The README calls itself an early in-progress draft; many service entries are incomplete and some sections are marked for correction
Pricing and support figures, market share, and the product tables reflect the dates the content was written (around 2016 to 2020) and may be outdated
It is a reference guide, not a tutorial, and does not include runnable setup steps
